---
title: "Introduction"
---


Dementia represents a major global health challenge, characterized by progressive cognitive decline that significantly impairs daily functioning and independence [@RN13; @RN32]. Worldwide prevalence is projected to reach 152 million by 2050, driven largely by population aging and increased life expectancy [@RN28], imposing an unprecedented burden on healthcare systems with global economic costs estimated at $15 trillion between 2020 and 2050 [@RN31]. Despite substantial research efforts, current therapeutic interventions remain largely ineffective [@RN3; @RN2], underscoring the critical need for early detection and prevention strategies [@RN35].

Epigenetic modifications, particularly DNA methylation, have emerged as key regulators of gene expression in neurodegenerative processes [@RN20; @RN37]. DNA methylation exhibits remarkable plasticity in response to environmental exposures and aging [@RN5; @RN21], potentially serving as a mechanistic link between risk factors and dementia pathogenesis [@RN34]. Epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) of brain tissue have revealed extensive methylation alterations associated with dementia pathology [@RN33; @RN23]. However, the inherent inaccessibility of brain tissue limits its utility for clinical monitoring, motivating the development of blood-based methylation biomarkers as a practical alternative [@RN43; @RN24]. Blood samples are readily obtained through minimally invasive procedures, enabling longitudinal monitoring and potential early detection [@RN11]. Accumulating evidence indicates that blood methylation patterns can reflect neurological processes [@RN19; @RN26; @RN37], and recent cross-sectional EWAS have identified blood-based differentially methylated positions (DMPs) in genes regulating synaptic plasticity, neuroinflammation, and lipid metabolism [@RN38; @RN39].

However, cross-tissue comparisons have revealed limited concordance between blood- and brain-based methylation signatures in dementia, with the majority of shared sites showing opposite directions of effect [@RN44], leaving it uncertain whether peripheral epigenetic patterns can adequately reflect neurodegenerative processes. Prior blood-based studies have additionally faced methodological limitations including restricted sample sizes [@RN39; @RN43; @RN42; @RN38; @RN36; @RN41], simplified dichotomous cognitive classifications [@RN39; @RN7; @RN43; @RN42; @RN36; @RN6; @RN40], and either absent [@RN39; @RN38; @RN41; @RN40] or limited [@RN7; @RN43; @RN42; @RN6] longitudinal follow-up. Together, these issues have impeded characterization of the dynamics of epigenetic modifications throughout disease progression, and the relationship between blood DNA methylation patterns and the diverse trajectories of cognitive decline remains poorly understood [@RN20].


Here, we conducted a large-scale longitudinal EWAS using baseline blood samples from 2,491 participants in the Age, Gene/Environment Susceptibility (AGES) Reykjavik Study [@RN1], with repeated cognitive assessments over up to 13.4 years of follow-up. This comprehensive dataset enabled characterization of methylation signatures associated with distinct cognitive trajectories, including transitions from normal cognition to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), stable MCI, and progression to dementia either directly from normal cognition or through an MCI intermediate stage. By leveraging detailed clinical categorization and extended follow-up, we aimed to examine whether blood-based epigenetic patterns associate with distinct trajectories of cognitive decline and may inform strategies for early detection and timely intervention.
